country.name: South Africa
country.tagline: Three and a half centuries of Cape wine, from Van Riebeeck's first pressing to Swartland old-vine Chenin, told in mountains, wind and granite.

stats.note: About 86,525 ha of wine grapes (WOSA, 2026); total vineyard including table and drying grapes 109 kha and wine production 10.2 mhl in 2025, seventh in the world (OIV, May 2026). SAWIS counted 2,176 grape producers and 507 cellars crushing grapes in 2025.

country.overview:
South African wine is the oldest in the New World outside the Americas, and the most complicated. On 2 February 1659, seven years after the Dutch East India Company (VOC) set up a supply station at the Cape, Commander Jan van Riebeeck wrote in his diary: 'Today, praise be to God, wine was pressed for the first time from Cape grapes.' Within thirty years Simon van der Stel had founded Constantia, whose sweet wine became one of the most famous in Europe, and French Huguenot refugees had settled the valley that is still called Franschhoek, 'French corner'. Much of the labour on these farms was enslaved, and the industry's history is bound up with slavery, dispossession and, later, apartheid; the wine story cannot be told honestly without that.

The modern industry has about 86,500 hectares of wine grapes, almost all in the Western Cape within a few hours of Cape Town. It is defined by the meeting of a Mediterranean climate with two oceans and a wall of mountains. The cold Benguela current up the west coast and the south-easterly 'Cape Doctor' wind cool vineyards that would otherwise be hot; the Cape Fold Belt's sandstone and granite mountains, some of the oldest soils on earth, give a mosaic of slopes, aspects and altitudes. Inland, behind the mountains, the Breede River Valley, Olifants River and Klein Karoo are hotter, drier and irrigated.

Chenin Blanc is the signature. Brought from the Loire in the seventeenth century, it is the most planted variety, roughly 18 percent of the vineyard and more than in any other country. For centuries it was the workhorse for brandy and bulk wine; today old bush-vine Chenin from the Swartland, Stellenbosch and the Olifants River makes some of the world's most exciting whites. South Africa also has its own grape, Pinotage, a 1925 cross of Pinot Noir and Cinsaut (then called Hermitage) by Abraham Perold, and world-class Bordeaux blends, Syrah, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc and traditional-method sparkling (Cap Classique). Its sweet wine history, from Vin de Constance to the 'Cape Port' styles of Calitzdorp, is equally rich.

The twentieth century was shaped by the KWV, the growers' co-operative founded in 1918 to fix minimum prices in a glutted market. From 1957 a quota system controlled what could be planted and where; it rewarded volume, kept most wine flowing to distillation, and froze the vineyard in old varieties and co-operative cellars. International sanctions against apartheid cut South African wine off from most export markets in the 1980s. The release of Nelson Mandela in 1990 and the democratic elections of 1994 reopened the world; quotas ended in 1992, the KWV became a company in 1997, and exports grew from a trickle to more than 300 million litres a year.

The past two decades brought a quality revolution. In the Swartland, Eben Sadie (Columella, 2000), Chris and Andrea Mullineux and Adi Badenhorst rediscovered old dry-farmed vineyards of Chenin, Grenache, Cinsault and Palomino; their Swartland Revolution festival (2010 to 2015) put a young, natural-leaning generation on the world stage. Rosa Kruger began mapping old vines, and the Old Vine Project now certifies vineyards over 35 years old with a 'Certified Heritage Vineyard' seal giving the planting year; in 2024 the OIV adopted the same 35-year benchmark for an 'old vine'. Cool sites in the Hemel-en-Aarde, Elgin and Elim have made South Africa a serious source of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

The challenges are real. Land and ownership remain overwhelmingly white, three decades after apartheid; black-owned brands, empowerment schemes and organisations such as the Pinotage Youth Development Academy and the Cape Winemakers Guild's protégé programme are growing but still small. The vineyard is shrinking (from over 100,000 ha in 2009), the 2015 to 2017 drought and 2020 Covid alcohol-sales bans hit hard, and prices remain low for the quality. Yet the 2025 harvest of 10.2 million hectolitres was a full recovery, and few countries offer so much old-vine character for the money.

history.title: Van Riebeeck's first wine
history.text: The VOC's Cape commander Jan van Riebeeck planted vines from 1655 and pressed the first Cape wine on 2 February 1659, recording it in his diary. Vines were grown partly to fight scurvy on the ships' crews.

history.title: Stellenbosch and Constantia
history.text: Commander Simon van der Stel founded Stellenbosch in 1679, the colony's second town, and in 1685 was granted Constantia, where he planted a large vineyard and made wine for the Company and the passing fleets.

history.title: The Huguenots arrive
history.text: About 200 French Protestant refugees, fleeing persecution after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes, were settled by the VOC in the Drakenstein and Franschhoek valleys. They brought viticultural knowledge and names (de Villiers, du Toit, Joubert, Malan, le Roux) that still run Cape farms.

history.title: Constantia's golden age
history.text: Hendrik Cloete bought Groot Constantia in 1778 and made an unfortified sweet Muscat wine that became the toast of European courts. Napoleon had it shipped to St Helena during his exile (1815 to 1821); Jane Austen recommended it for a broken heart in Sense and Sensibility (1811), and Baudelaire and Dickens wrote about it.

history.title: Emancipation
history.text: Slavery was abolished in the Cape in 1834 (with a four-year 'apprenticeship'). The 'dop' system of paying farm workers partly in wine, which caused generations of harm, persisted long after and was only outlawed in 1960, though it lingered informally.

history.title: Phylloxera
history.text: Phylloxera was found near Mowbray, Cape Town, in 1886 and spread through the winelands, destroying most vineyards. Replanting on American rootstocks favoured high-yielding varieties such as Cinsaut.

history.title: The KWV
history.text: The Koöperatieve Wijnbouwers Vereniging van Zuid-Afrika (KWV) was founded at Paarl in 1918 to stabilise prices in a glutted market. Statutory powers from 1924 and a quota system from 1957 let it control prices and plantings until the 1990s.

history.title: Pinotage
history.text: Professor Abraham Izak Perold crossed Pinot Noir with Cinsaut (then called Hermitage) at Welgevallen, Stellenbosch University's experimental farm, in 1925. The first wine was made at Elsenburg in 1941, and a Bellevue Pinotage won the Cape Wine Show in 1959; in 1961 it became the first wine labelled Pinotage.

history.title: First Cap Classique
history.text: Frans Malan of Simonsig made Kaapse Vonkel, the first South African bottle-fermented sparkling wine, from the 1971 vintage. The category is now called Méthode Cap Classique.

history.title: Wine of Origin
history.text: The Wine of Origin scheme came into force in 1973, defining regions, districts and wards and certifying origin, variety and vintage claims. Every certified bottle carries a Wine and Spirit Board seal.

history.title: Reopening to the world
history.text: Nelson Mandela's release in 1990 and the elections of 1994 ended apartheid-era sanctions. Exports rose quickly; the KWV's quota system ended in 1992 and the co-operative became a company in 1997.

history.title: Columella and the Swartland
history.text: Eben Sadie made the first Columella, a Syrah-Mourvèdre blend, in 2000 (about 5,000 bottles), followed by Palladius white in 2002. The Swartland became the centre of a new generation of old-vine, low-intervention wines.

history.title: Swartland Revolution
history.text: Sadie, the Mullineuxs, Adi Badenhorst and Callie Louw (Porseleinberg) launched the Swartland Revolution festival at Riebeek-Kasteel, which ran until 2015 and drew wine writers from around the world.

history.title: Old Vine Project
history.text: Rosa Kruger began cataloguing old vineyards in 2002; the Old Vine Project's Certified Heritage Vineyard seal marks vineyards at least 35 years old with their planting date. In 2024 the OIV adopted 35 years as the global definition of an old vine.

history.title: Drought and lockdowns
history.text: The 2015 to 2017 drought shrank Western Cape harvests and the vineyard, and Covid-era bans on alcohol sales and exports in 2020 cost the industry heavily. The 2025 harvest (10.2 mhl) marked a full recovery.

country.classification:
The Wine of Origin (WO) scheme, in force since 1973 and administered by the Wine and Spirit Board, certifies three claims on a label: origin, grape variety and vintage. If a variety or vintage is named, at least 85 percent of the wine must be that variety or year; an origin claim requires 100 percent of the grapes from the named area. Every certified bottle carries a numbered seal.

Origins nest in a hierarchy that has grown more complex over time. The February 2026 list starts with the overarching geographical unit Greater Cape (Western, Northern and Eastern Cape) and six other geographical units (KwaZulu-Natal, Free State, Limpopo, North West and, oddly, a 'none' unit for the Lanseria ward). Inside the Western Cape are the overarching region Cape Coast (Coastal Region plus Cape South Coast) and the regions Breede River Valley, Klein Karoo and Olifants River; the Northern Cape holds the Karoo-Hoogland region. A newer subregion layer, Cape West Coast, groups Darling, Lutzville Valley, St Helena Bay and the coastal wards. Below these are districts (for example Stellenbosch, Paarl, Swartland, Walker Bay) and, at the smallest scale, wards (Simonsberg-Stellenbosch, Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, Piekenierskloof). Some wards sit outside any district (Cederberg, Elim's neighbours Napier and Herbertsdale, Lamberts Bay). In total WOSA counts 32 districts and about 100 wards.

Units are defined mostly by geography rather than by proven style, and like the Australian and New Zealand systems the scheme sets no rules on varieties or yields. Two other labels matter: 'Estate Wine', a term for wine grown, made and bottled on registered contiguous land, and the Old Vine Project's Certified Heritage Vineyard seal, which gives the planting year of vineyards at least 35 years old. The Integrated Production of Wine (IPW) sustainability scheme can be combined with the WO seal. 'Cape Port' and 'Cape Sherry' terms were retired under the EU trade agreement from 2012: fortified styles are now labelled Cape Vintage, Cape Ruby, Cape Tawny and Cape White, and Boberg is a historic designation for fortified wines from Paarl, Franschhoek and Tulbagh.
country.climate_soils:
The Cape winelands have a Mediterranean climate of wet winters and dry summers, but the details are set by oceans and mountains. The cold Benguela current runs up the Atlantic coast, cooling the west coast (Darling, Lamberts Bay, Bamboes Bay) and bringing fog. The strong south-easterly wind of summer, the 'Cape Doctor', blows off False Bay and Walker Bay, cooling Stellenbosch, Constantia, Elgin and the Hemel-en-Aarde, keeping disease down and thickening grape skins. Away from the sea and behind the mountain ranges, temperatures rise and rainfall falls sharply: from about 1,000 mm a year in Constantia and Stellenbosch to 250 to 400 mm in Robertson, the Klein Karoo and the Olifants River, where irrigation is essential.

Geologically the Cape is ancient. Granite intrusions about 550 million years old underlie Stellenbosch, Paarl and the Paardeberg; Table Mountain sandstone forms the high ranges and the poor, sandy soils of Cederberg and Elgin; Malmesbury shale, even older, weathers to the dark 'schist' soils of the Swartland and Tygerberg; Bokkeveld shale is found in the Hemel-en-Aarde and Klein Karoo. Robertson has unusual lime-rich soils along the Breede River. Mostly low in nutrients and naturally acidic, these soils are good at restraining vigour, and the many slopes, aspects and altitudes (from sea level to Sutherland's vineyards at about 1,500 m) give the Cape far more variety than its latitude (roughly 32 to 35 degrees south) would suggest.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc
grapes.note: The most planted variety (about 18 percent of the vineyard). Once brandy and bulk fodder, now made in every style from crisp and fruity to barrel-fermented old-vine wines of great depth, and in sweet and sparkling forms.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.note: The leading red grape, especially in Stellenbosch, where Bordeaux blends (Meerlust Rubicon, Kanonkop Paul Sauer, Vergelegen V) are classics.

grapes.name: Colombard
grapes.note: Widely planted inland for brandy, bulk wine and fresh, inexpensive whites.

grapes.name: Shiraz / Syrah
grapes.note: Grown everywhere; peppery and fresh from the Swartland and Hemel-en-Aarde, richer from Stellenbosch and Paarl.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.note: Cool-climate styles from Constantia, Durbanville, Elgin, Elim and the west coast.

grapes.name: Pinotage
grapes.note: South Africa's own cross of Pinot Noir and Cinsaut (1925). Best from old bush vines (Kanonkop, Beyerskloof, Kaapzicht) and in Cape Blends with Bordeaux varieties.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.note: Fine and mineral from the Hemel-en-Aarde, Elgin and Robertson's limestone.

grapes.name: Cinsault, Grenache, Palomino, Sémillon
grapes.note: Old plantings rediscovered by the new wave; Cinsault (once the main red) now makes light, fragrant wines, and Sémillon Gris survives in old Franschhoek vineyards.

grapes.name: Muscat de Frontignan and Muscat d'Alexandrie
grapes.note: Behind Vin de Constance and the fortified 'Muscadel' wines of Robertson and the Klein Karoo.

grapes.name: Touriga Nacional and Tinta Barocca
grapes.note: The base of Calitzdorp's Cape Vintage and Cape Tawny fortified wines.

regions.name: Coastal Region
regions.tagline: Stellenbosch, Paarl, Swartland and Constantia: the historic heart of Cape wine, within an hour of Cape Town.
regions.summary: The Coastal Region holds most of South Africa's famous names: the districts of Cape Town (with Constantia and Durbanville), Stellenbosch, Paarl, Franschhoek, Wellington, Swartland, Tulbagh, Darling and Lutzville Valley. It is defined by proximity to the Atlantic and False Bay, whose cool air and the summer south-easter moderate a warm Mediterranean climate.
regions.history: Every chapter of Cape wine history begins here: Van Riebeeck's garden in Cape Town (1659), Constantia (1685), the Huguenot farms of Franschhoek and Drakenstein (1688), the KWV at Paarl (1918), Pinotage at Stellenbosch (1925) and the Swartland Revolution (2010).
regions.terroir: Granite and sandstone mountains (Simonsberg, Helderberg, Paardeberg, Drakenstein) with shale and sandstone-derived soils on the lower slopes; rainfall from about 1,000 mm near False Bay to under 450 mm in the Swartland.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Chenin Blanc, Shiraz, Pinotage, Merlot, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Cinsault, Grenache.
regions.styles: Bordeaux blends, Cape Blends with Pinotage, old-vine Chenin and Rhône blends, Cap Classique, Vin de Constance.
regions.classification: Region within the overarching Cape Coast region; districts Cape Town, Darling, Franschhoek, Lutzville Valley, Paarl, Stellenbosch, Swartland, Tulbagh, Wellington; Cape West Coast subregion overlaps its western part.

regions.name: Cape South Coast
regions.tagline: The cool southern rim of Africa, where Pinot Noir and Chardonnay found a home.
regions.summary: Stretching east from Elgin along the coast to Plettenberg Bay, the Cape South Coast region contains South Africa's coolest wine country: Elgin, Walker Bay (with the Hemel-en-Aarde wards), Cape Agulhas (Elim), Overberg, Swellendam, Still Bay, Lower Duivenhoks River and Plettenberg Bay. Most of its vineyards are less than 50 years old.
regions.history: Apart from scattered farms, wine came late: Tim Hamilton Russell planted in the Hemel-en-Aarde Valley in 1975, Elgin's apple farmers turned to vines from the late 1980s, and the Elim and Plettenberg Bay vineyards date from the late 1990s and 2000s.
regions.terroir: Strong maritime influence, persistent sea winds and cool, cloudy summers; soils of Bokkeveld shale, Table Mountain sandstone and decomposed granite.
regions.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Shiraz, Chenin Blanc, Sémillon.
regions.styles: Burgundy-style Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, cool Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon, Cap Classique.
regions.classification: Region within the overarching Cape Coast region; districts Cape Agulhas, Elgin, Lower Duivenhoks River, Overberg, Plettenberg Bay, Swellendam, Walker Bay, Still Bay; wards outside districts: Herbertsdale, Napier.

regions.name: Breede River Valley
regions.tagline: The broad, irrigated engine of Cape wine and brandy, with Robertson's limestone as its fine-wine jewel.
regions.summary: East of the Du Toitskloof and Hex River mountains, the Breede River Valley region (Breedekloof, Worcester and Robertson districts) grows a large share of South Africa's grapes for wine, brandy and grape juice. Its co-operative cellars were the backbone of the quota era; today they bottle good-value wines, and Robertson's estates make some of the country's best Chardonnay and Cap Classique.
regions.history: Settled in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries as stock and grain country, the valley grew with irrigation schemes in the twentieth century. Worcester is South Africa's brandy capital, and Robertson's De Wetshof and Graham Beck put the district on the fine-wine map in the 1970s to 1990s.
regions.terroir: Hot, dry summers (300 to 400 mm of rain in Robertson) moderated by south-easterly winds funnelling up the valley; alluvial soils along the river and lime-rich soils in Robertson.
regions.grapes: Chenin Blanc, Colombard, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Muscadel.
regions.styles: Fresh whites, Chardonnay, Cap Classique, brandy base, fortified Muscadel.
regions.classification: Region with districts Breedekloof (wards Goudini, Slanghoek), Robertson (14 wards) and Worcester (7 wards).

regions.name: Klein Karoo
regions.tagline: Ostrich farms, mountain passes and South Africa's finest port-style wines.
regions.summary: A long, semi-arid valley between the Langeberg and Swartberg ranges along Route 62, from Montagu to the Langkloof. Vines grow in kloofs and river valleys. The region is best known for Calitzdorp's fortified wines in the Portuguese style and for Muscadel, but cooler, higher wards (Tradouw Highlands, Upper Langkloof, Outeniqua, Koo Plateau) make fine table wines.
regions.history: Calitzdorp's Nel family (Boplaas and De Krans) planted Touriga Nacional and Tinta Barocca and built the Cape's reputation for 'Cape Port'; the term was retired in 2012 under the EU agreement in favour of Cape Vintage, Cape Ruby and Cape Tawny.
regions.terroir: Hot days, cold nights and very low rainfall; Bokkeveld shale and alluvium, with Table Mountain sandstone in the ranges.
regions.grapes: Muscat, Touriga Nacional, Tinta Barocca, Souzão, Chenin Blanc, Colombard, Shiraz.
regions.styles: Cape Vintage, Cape Tawny, Cape Ruby, Muscadel, potstill brandy.
regions.classification: Region with districts Calitzdorp (ward Groenfontein) and Langeberg-Garcia; wards outside districts Cango Valley, Koo Plateau, Montagu, Outeniqua, Tradouw, Tradouw Highlands, Upper Langkloof.

regions.name: Olifants River
regions.tagline: From the high sandstone of Piekenierskloof to the huge co-operatives of Vredendal.
regions.summary: The Olifants River valley runs north from the Piekenierskloof Pass past Citrusdal and Clanwilliam to the Atlantic near Lutzville. It is citrus and rooibos country with large irrigated vineyards in the lower valley (Vredendal, Spruitdrift) and old, dry-farmed bush vines in the mountains (Piekenierskloof, Skurfberg) that new-wave winemakers prize for Grenache, Chenin and Palomino.
regions.history: Irrigation from the Clanwilliam Dam (1930s) created the lower valley's large cellars; Namaqua Wines at Vredendal is among the biggest in the country.
regions.terroir: Warm and dry, with sandy soils from Table Mountain sandstone in the mountains and red clay loams on the valley floor.
regions.grapes: Chenin Blanc, Colombard, Grenache, Pinotage, Shiraz, Palomino.
regions.styles: Value whites and reds; old-vine Grenache and Chenin from the mountains.
regions.classification: Region with districts Citrusdal Mountain (ward Piekenierskloof) and Citrusdal Valley; wards Spruitdrift and Vredendal.

regions.name: Cape West Coast
regions.tagline: Fog, cold Atlantic air and some of the Cape's most windswept vineyards.
regions.summary: A subregion created after a 2019 proposal to group the vineyards nearest the Atlantic: the Darling and Lutzville Valley districts, St Helena Bay (in Swartland) and the wards of Bamboes Bay and Lamberts Bay. The cold Benguela current and morning fog make these some of the coolest sites in the Western Cape for their latitude.
regions.history: Mostly planted since the 1990s; Fryer's Cove at Bamboes Bay and Groote Post at Darling were pioneers of cool west coast Sauvignon Blanc.
regions.terroir: Sandy and granite-derived soils, strong sea winds, low rainfall and fog.
regions.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chenin Blanc, Pinotage, Shiraz.
regions.classification: Subregion of the Coastal Region (and listed under it on the February 2026 schedule).

regions.name: Northern Cape
regions.tagline: Desert vineyards on the Orange River and the highest vines in South Africa at Sutherland.
regions.summary: The Northern Cape geographical unit includes the irrigated vineyards along the Orange River around Upington (the Central Orange River district), the Douglas and Hartswater areas, and the Karoo-Hoogland region, whose Sutherland-Karoo district grows grapes near South Africa's coldest town at about 1,500 m.
regions.history: Irrigation along the Orange River from the early twentieth century created a large table-grape and raisin industry; wine cellars such as Orange River Cellars grew from it.
regions.terroir: Hot, arid and irrigated along the river; cold and high on the Karoo plateau.
regions.grapes: Colombard, Chenin Blanc, Muscat d'Alexandrie, Pinotage, Shiraz.
regions.styles: Everyday whites, sweet Muscat, some reds.
regions.classification: Geographical unit within Greater Cape; region Karoo-Hoogland (district Sutherland-Karoo); districts Central Orange River and Douglas; wards Hartswater and Prieska.
